name: Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord
summary: Talleyrand favoured constitutional monarchy, commercial exchange and a European balance of power. His advocacy of civil liberties coexisted with women’s political exclusion and support for colonial settlement. He served successive regimes and opposed parts of Napoleon’s expansionist policy.

sources.title: Speeches on ecclesiastical property (1789), banking (1789) and press freedom (1821), reproduced in Reminiscences of Prince Talleyrand, II
sources.author: Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord; collection edited by Madame Colmache (1848)
sources.usedFor: Published speech texts; distinguished from biographical anecdotes and problematic letter dating.

sources.title: Rapport sur l’Instruction Publique, 10, 11 and 19 September 1791
sources.author: Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord
sources.usedFor: Full education programme, including fees, gender exclusions, morality and religion.

sources.title: Essai sur les avantages à retirer de colonies nouvelles (1797), reproduced in Essai sur Talleyrand
sources.author: Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord; Henry Lytton Bulwer, translated by Georges Perrot
sources.usedFor: Full colonial essay and accompanying political-economy address.

sources.title: Extrait des registres du Sénat-conservateur, 6 April 1814
sources.author: French Senate; constitution proposed by the provisional government led by Talleyrand
sources.usedFor: Constitutional settlement he personally promoted; article-specific support receives medium confidence.

sources.title: Talleyrand, une vision européenne
sources.author: Emmanuel de Waresquiel, Fondation Napoléon
sources.usedFor: Career-long trade, colonial and diplomatic strategy, including late support for retaining Algeria.

sources.title: Talleyrand, Napoleonic Satires
sources.author: Brown University Library
sources.usedFor: Early career, church reform and constitutional monarchy.

notes: Full education and colonial reports and collected speech texts were downloaded and searched by theme. Constitutional answers concern a settlement he personally promoted, not mere assent. The 1821 press speech outweighs earlier service under censorship. His colonial position is qualified by his opposition to domination; his later Algerian policy prevents treating him as uniformly opposed to expansion. Reprinted speech documents are primary; biographers’ reports receive medium confidence at most.
